 - Advertisement - 
 The pimple may be gone, but the dark spot it left behind can linger for months. For people with darker skin tones, that’s often one of the most frustrating parts of acne.
 Inflammation from a breakout can trigger excess pigment production, leaving behind flat brown, dark brown, or bluish-gray spots known as post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH). Deeper acne can lead to permanent scarring. That’s why treating acne early matters. Delaying treatment can allow breakouts to worsen and increase the risk of lasting skin changes. Early treatment can help prevent new acne and reduce the dark spots and scars it may leave behind.
 So, when is an over-the-counter routine enough, and when should you see a dermatologist?
 Acne Can Look Different on Darker Skin
 Acne develops when pores become clogged with oil and dead skin cells. It can show up as blackheads, whiteheads, pimples, or those annoying deeper, painful bumps called nodules.
 On darker skin, inflammation may not always look bright red. Depending on your skin tone, an inflamed breakout may appear dark red, purple, brown, or simply darker than the surrounding skin.
 - Advertisement - 
 After the breakout heals, PIH may remain. And while the discoloration often fades over time, preventing new breakouts is one of the most important ways to prevent new dark spots from forming.
 Before You Buy Another Acne Product…
 If the dark marks are what bothers you most, it can be tempting to focus only on fading them. But treating the acne that caused them is just as important.
 And whatever you do, don’t pop that pimple! Picking and squeezing can worsen inflammation, increasing your risk of both hyperpigmentation and permanent scarring.
 The good news is that mild acne — such as blackheads, whiteheads, and occasional pimples — can often be managed with over-the-counter products. A few ingredients you want to look for:
 Adapalene: helps unclog pores and prevent new breakouts 5 
 Benzoyl peroxide: reduces acne-causing bacteria and can help treat inflammatory acne
 Salicylic acid: helps unclog pores
 Azelaic acid: can treat acne while also helping fade the dark spots it leaves behind
 But don’t start everything at once! Overloading your skin with active ingredients can cause irritation. In melanin-rich skin, that irritation can lead to more hyperpigmentation.
 Instead, keep your routine simple: use a gentle cleanser, introduce acne treatments gradually, moisturize, and choose skin-care and makeup products labeled noncomedogenic, meaning they’re formulated not to clog pores. 4 
 Then give your treatment time to work. Acne improvement takes weeks, not days.
 5 Signs It’s Time to See a Dermatologist
 You don’t have to wait until your acne becomes severe. In some cases, seeing a dermatologist earlier can help prevent lasting skin changes.
 1. Your Acne Is Deep or Painful
 Large, tender bumps beneath the skin are harder to treat with drugstore products alone and are more likely to leave scars. If you’re developing deep, painful nodules, consider seeing a dermatologist early rather than repeatedly trying new over-the-counter products.
 2. You’re Starting to Scar
 A dark spot isn’t necessarily a scar. What’s the difference? PIH changes skin color while acne scars alter skin texture, creating indentations or raised areas.
 Once you notice scarring, controlling active acne becomes especially important, as preventing new scars is easier than treating established ones.
 3. Every Breakout Leaves a Dark Mark
 If you’re constantly treating yesterday’s dark spots while new acne creates tomorrow’s, it’s time to address both issues at once
 A dermatologist can help develop a regimen that controls acne that causes the marks while also addressing existing hyperpigmentation, without unnecessarily irritating your skin.
 4. Your Acne Isn’t Improving
 If you’ve consistently used an appropriate over-the-counter regimen for six to eight weeks and you’re still breaking out, you may need prescription treatment. 5 
 A dermatologist can also determine whether those bumps are actually acne or another skin condition that requires a different approach.
 5. Your Skin Is Affecting How You Feel
 You don’t need severe acne to justify seeing a dermatologist.
 Acne can affect confidence, self-esteem, and overall quality of life. Sometimes that impact goes beyond how your skin looks. It can change how comfortable you feel in social situations, when being photographed, when meeting new people, or when going out without makeup.
 If you find yourself thinking about your skin constantly, avoiding things you normally enjoy or simply feeling stressed about your appearance, it’s reasonable to seek treatment. How acne makes you feel matters, too.
 What Can a Dermatologist Do?
 A dermatologist can tailor treatment to your type of acne and your individual skin concerns.
 Prescription options may include topical retinoids, oral antibiotics, hormonal treatments such as certain birth control pills or spironolactone, or isotretinoin (Accutane) for severe or treatment-resistant acne.
 For darker skin tones, a dermatologist can also help treat the acne that drives new dark spots while addressing the hyperpigmentation already present. They can also help distinguish PIH from true acne scarring, which matters because the treatments aren’t necessarily the same.
 And if you’re considering procedures such as chemical peels or lasers for dark spots or acne scars, seek professional guidance first. When procedures aren’t selected or performed appropriately, they can cause unwanted pigment changes in darker skin. A board-certified dermatologist with experience treating skin of color can help determine which options are appropriate for you.
 Sunscreen Is Not Optional
 If you’re treating acne or trying to fade dark spots but skipping sunscreen, you may be working against your own progress.
 Darker skin contains more melanin, which provides some natural protection from ultraviolet radiation, but it doesn’t make skin immune to sun damage. Sun exposure can worsen existing hyperpigmentation, and visible light can also contribute to discoloration in darker skin tones.
 That’s where sunscreen comes in. Use a broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher every day. If dark spots are a major concern, consider a tinted sunscreen containing iron oxides, which can provide additional protection against visible light.
 If you’re acne-prone, look for a sunscreen labeled noncomedogenic or “won’t clog pores.” Tinted or sheer formulations can also help minimize the white or chalky cast that some sunscreens leave on deeper complexions. 9 
 The Bottom Line
 Acne doesn’t have to become severe before you ask for help.
 Treating breakouts early can also help prevent hyperpigmentation and scarring that may persist long after the acne has cleared.
 If your acne is painful, leaves scars or persistent dark spots, affects your confidence, or doesn’t improve with over-the-counter treatments, consider seeing a dermatologist.
 Clearing acne is only part of the goal. Preventing what it leaves behind — both visible and not — matters, too.
